# R2 Digest — Prologue 1 + Part 1a (Jer 1–4 mostly)

**Source:** John Goldingay, *The Book of Jeremiah*, NICOT  
**Slice:** `.cache/goldingay-jeremiah-reingest-2026-07-18/slices/R2_prol_p1a_2713-5300.txt`  
**Raw range:** 2713–5300 (slice lines 1–~2588; text ends mid-4:31)  
**Scope:** Prologue 1:1–19 (call; almond; boiling pot); Part One intro; 2:1–37 marriage/confrontation; 3:1–4:4 *šûb* turning; 4:5–31 war/desolation warnings (partial)  
**Extractor:** R2 only. No wiki edits. No task-observer.

### C-R2-01
**Claim:** Goldingay reads Jer 1 as a four-part scroll introduction (vv. 1–3 preface; 4–10 commission; 11–12 almond message; 13–19 boiling-pot disaster + renewed commission), coherent though assembled from originally separate elements, with MT section markers after vv. 3, 6, 10, 12, 19.
**Quote:** “Jeremiah 1 thus forms a coherent section to introduce the scroll. It does so by bringing together some originally separate elements.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 8–47; Jer 1:1–19
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-02
**Claim:** The third-person preface (1:1–3) answers who Jeremiah was, where his message came from, and what it was about; Goldingay attributes it to “theologian-curators” (conventionally “Deuteronomists”) who “impose order on chaos” and hint at prophetic line replacing defunct priestly/kingly lines.
**Quote:** “It functions to ‘impose order on chaos’—on ‘the messy and terrible events of history’… and it hints at the replacement of defunct priestly and kingly lines by a prophetic line.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 72–84; Jer 1:1–3
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-03
**Claim:** Jeremiah of Anathoth is a Benjaminite/northern figure three miles north of Jerusalem; Goldingay finds it tempting to link his priestly family to Abiathar banished by Solomon—so “from the place to which Solomon banished Abiathar comes a man who will speak the word against Solomon’s edifice”—and notes possible Anathoth–Jerusalem priestly crossfire (Jer 11–12).
**Quote:** “Ironically, then, from the place to which Solomon banished Abiathar comes a man who will speak the word against Solomon’s edifice.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 87–88; Jer 1:1
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-04
**Claim:** “Yahweh’s message came” (*hāyâ*) marks a “word event”—objective incursion of potent word, not Jeremiah’s wise reflection; the words of Jeremiah (v. 1) are also Yahweh’s message; initial coming in Josiah’s thirteenth year = 626 BC.
**Quote:** “The expression *Yahweh’s message came* suggests a ‘word event’ that represents ‘the incursion of potent, sovereign word into the life of prophet and nation.’”
**Locus:** slice ll. 90–91; Jer 1:2
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-05
**Claim:** The preface ends at the exile of Jerusalem (fifth month), not Zedekiah’s personal end; paired with ch. 52 this buttresses Jeremiah as true prophet. The preface “knows” the city will fall; the scroll is for people who know exile has happened and need to understand it and look to the future.
**Quote:** “Whether the city will fall is an open question through most of the scroll, but the preface knows that it will. And the scroll is written for people who know that the exile has happened…”
**Locus:** slice ll. 94–96; Jer 1:3
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-06
**Claim:** Goldingay notes the relative thinness of Josiah’s reformation in the scroll: its early failure and post-Josiah reversion made the reformation “hardly a dynamic to draw attention to” for later generations.
**Quote:** “As the Jeremiah scroll sought to bring its challenging and encouraging message to the next generation or three, the failure of Josiah’s reformation was hardly a dynamic to draw attention to.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 100–102; Jer 1:1–3
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-07
**Claim:** The commission (1:4–10) is not a “call” with vocational baggage: Yahweh’s initiative antedates birth; Jeremiah is no volunteer like Isaiah; no sense of vocation-seeking; if vocation is Buechner’s gladness-meets-hunger, Jeremiah has none—“a call to dissent.”
**Quote:** “If vocation is ‘the place where your deep gladness and the world’s deep hunger meet,’ Jeremiah has no vocation, or his vocation is ‘a call to dissent.’”
**Locus:** slice ll. 205–207; Jer 1:4–10
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-08
**Claim:** *Yādaʿ* in 1:5 is “acknowledge/choose”—commitment before existence, not mere taking responsibility; “choice” vs “acknowledgment”: Yahweh made a commitment to Jeremiah before he existed; designation is unique in the First Testament (paralleled by Jesus in Luke 1; Paul generalizes in Rom 8:29).
**Quote:** “But ‘choice’ simply implies taking responsibility, whereas ‘acknowledgment’ implies making a commitment… Yahweh made a commitment to Jeremiah before Jeremiah existed.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 330–331; Jer 1:5
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-09
**Claim:** Sanctifying (*qādaš* hiphil) claims Jeremiah like firstborn; nearest Jeremianic parallel is sanctifying warriors; also priestly consecration resonance from Anathoth lineage—both Jeremiah and Ezekiel have priestly lineage, cannot function as temple priests, and are appointed prophets by consecration.
**Quote:** “Jeremiah is especially claimed by God, like the firstborn of human beings and animals… Both prophets had priestly lineage; neither prophet could function as a priest in the temple; both are appointed as prophets by an act of consecration.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 336; Jer 1:5
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-10
**Claim:** “The nations’ prophet” is a “very strange designation”; role means judgment against the world of nations *and* that they may turn and be built/planted; addressed mainly to Judah’s kings/cabinet/priests/people about foreign and religious policy, not usually to the nations themselves.
**Quote:** “The Jeremiah scroll as a whole will suggest developing the idea of the nations’ prophet in at least two directions: It means Yahweh’s judgment is coming against the entire world of nations. It also means that they may turn to Yahweh and thus be built and planted.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 339–341; Jer 1:5b
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-11
**Claim:** Jeremiah’s “I’m a kid” (*naʿar*) objects to lack of expertise/training/gifting for speaking, not mere youth; unpoetic panic rhetoric establishes he is not inclined by himself to wrath-message; Yahweh answers by clarifying go/speak whatever ordered (Deut 18:18 prophet-like-Moses correspondence).
**Quote:** “his point concerns not his youthfulness but his lack of expertise, training, or gifting… This complementary colon corresponds to Yahweh’s promise concerning a prophet like Moses.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 344–350; Jer 1:6–7
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-12
**Claim:** Touching the mouth (1:9) is performative: puts Yahweh’s words in mouth once-for-all so Jeremiah externalizes Yahweh’s perspective (contrast Ezekiel internalizing by eating scroll; Isaiah’s coal cleanses); implements pre-birth plan with *nātan* matching “I am making.”
**Quote:** “The action in Jeremiah suggests that Yahweh causes Jeremiah to externalize his perspective. It is a performative action… Yahweh is here doing so in a once-for-all way for Jeremiah.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 372; Jer 1:9
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-13
**Claim:** Six infinitives (pull up/down, wipe out/smash, build/plant) leave subject and object open (Jeremiah? nations? Yahweh? Israel?); balance is more hopeful than Jeremiah’s actual messages—encouraging for post-destruction readers; the scroll “walks Jews into, through, and beyond” exile via plant/build.
**Quote:** “At its very outset, the Jeremiah scroll, ‘which is so preoccupied with “exile” … can anticipate the destruction of Babylon and the restoration of Jerusalem in the word pair “plant and build.”’ The scroll is ‘designed to walk Jews into, through, and beyond the reality of destruction and exile.’”
**Locus:** slice ll. 375–379; Jer 1:10
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-14
**Claim:** Demolition/uprooting and building/planting remain open alternatives (repentance or ruin) until 587 closes the future; Yahweh’s words leave open whether they are choices, sequential experiences, or de facto paths for recalcitrant vs repentant.
**Quote:** “Whereas in v. 3, with hindsight, the future was closed, here it is open. ‘The choice before us,’ Jeremiah would urge, is ‘repentance or ruin.’”
**Locus:** slice ll. 382; Jer 1:10
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-15
**Claim:** Almond/watcher cane (1:11–12): paronomasia *šāqēd*/*šāqad*—not primarily blossom symbolism; Yahweh keeps watch over his message to act on it; not necessarily soon; significant given long gap between declarations and actions; watching is God’s responsibility, not Jeremiah’s.
**Quote:** “More likely, his point depends on a paronomasia: the tree’s name happens to recall the word for keeping watch… He does not declare the intention to act soon. Rather, he is promising definitely to act in due course.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 402–405; Jer 1:11–12
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-16
**Claim:** Boiling/fanned pot (1:13–16): assonance *nāpûaḥ*/*ṣāpônâ* and *pātaḥ*—dire trouble opens out from the north; northern motif is political and supra-political (divine abode); Babylon not named until 20:4–6 / identified 25:9; threat is “greater than any human enemy.”
**Quote:** “The absence of a historical referent for the ‘boiling pot, tilted from the north,’ at the beginning of the book strikes an ominous note and is all the more fearsome for its lack of specificity. The threat from the north is greater than any human enemy.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 501–503; Jer 1:13–14
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-17
**Claim:** Northern kingdoms set thrones at Jerusalem’s gates to issue Yahweh’s *mišpāṭ* (authoritative decisions); *rāʿâ* names both dire action (unfaithfulness) and dire consequences—“naturally” linked or ensured by Yahweh. Three charges: abandoned me; burned offerings to other gods; bowed to things hands made (// Huldah 2 Kgs 22:17).
**Quote:** “Jeremiah frequently uses the same word (*rāʿâ*) to denote both what is dire in the latter sense (the action) and what is dire in the former sense (the consequences), suggesting that the consequences issue ‘naturally’ from the action or that Yahweh ensures that they do.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 506–509; Jer 1:15–16
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-18
**Claim:** Renewed commission (1:17–19): if Jeremiah breaks down psychologically, Yahweh will break him down physically; performative making as fortified town, iron pillar, bronze walls against kings, officials, priests, people of the land—Jeremiah “the true invincible city” while Judah’s towns fall; opposition because they oppose Yahweh’s word he embodies.

### C-R2-19
**Claim:** Goldingay’s best guess on composition of 1:4–19: theologian wrote 1:1–3; Jeremiah dictated 4–19 as mature reflection on youthful experience (580s/570s) adapted as introduction; whoever authored it, inspired portrayal for scroll readers. Goldingay rejects reductionism: “‘God’ is not a device for objectifying inner convictions.”
**Quote:** “The most plausible scenario is that a theologian wrote Jer 1:1–3, that Jeremiah dictated vv. 4–19… Verses 4–19 are then ‘a mature reflection on a youthful experience.’”
**Locus:** slice ll. 223–254; Jer 1:4–19
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R2-20
**Claim:** Part One (2:1–6:30) is a compilation confronting, warning, urging turn, promising restoration; focus rotates by chapter blocks (2 confrontation; 3:1–4:4 exhortation; 4:5–31 / 6 warnings; 5 confrontation); object throughout is to get Judah to turn. Heuristically linked to Jer 36 dictation for Jehoiakim’s time (Egypt overlord; post-Josiah reversion).
**Quote:** “Although the compilation thus includes only one section that comprises explicit exhortation… the object throughout is to get Judah to turn.”

### C-R2-21
**Claim:** Jer 2 is “a monologue of an abandoned God,” not an established speech form: kaleidoscope of images (husband/bride, vine, master/servant, path/camel/donkey); attributes claims/denials to Judah; moves speaker (Yahweh/Jeremiah) and addressee (feminine city, masculine nation, plural people).
**Quote:** “The chapter as a whole is not an established form of speech but a monologue of an abandoned God.”
**Locus:** slice ll. 745–748; Jer 2 intro
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[divine-human-marriage]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

- **Voice:** all claims attributed to Goldingay’s commentary on Jeremiah text; no outside synthesis presented as source content.
